The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in
$\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and therefore depend only on the corresponding
almost-everywhere classes.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Assume countable choice. For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $a,b\in\mathbb R^n$, and invertible real $n\times n$ matrix $A$, put $\tau_af(x)=f(x-a)$ and $M_bf(x)=e^{2\pi ib\cdot x}f(x)$. Then, at every frequency,
$$\widehat{\tau_af}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi ia\cdot\xi}\widehat f(\xi),\qquad\widehat{M_bf}(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi-b),\qquad\widehat{f\circ A}(\xi)=|\det A|^{-1}\widehat f(A^{-T}\xi).$$
Also $\widehat{f(-\cdot)}(\xi)=\widehat f(-\xi)$ and $\widehat{\overline f}(\xi)=\overline{\widehat f(-\xi)}$.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, and let
$H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion of
[[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical embedding
$E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Write
$\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ for the Japanese bracket, $\mathcal F$
for the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform, and
$u_g(\phi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}g(\xi)\phi(\xi)\,d\xi$ for the regular tempered
distribution of $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. Define
$$\mathcal W_s=\bigl\{u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n):\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu=u_g \text{ in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)\text{ for some }g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)\bigr\}.$$
Then:

1. The canonical embedding restricts to a bijection
   $E_s:H^s(\mathbb R^n)\to\mathcal W_s$. Thus, after identifying a completion
   class with its image under $E_s$, $H^s(\mathbb R^n)$ is **exactly** the set
   of tempered distributions whose bracket-weighted Fourier transform is the
   regular distribution of an $L^2$ class, and that class $g$ is unique.
2. The norm identity is exact:
$$\|U\|_{H^s}=\|g\|_2=\bigl\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)\bigr\|_2 \qquad(U\in H^s),$$
   where the last expression means the $L^2$ norm of the unique density $g$ of
   the distributional product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)$, and the
   defining completion norm $q_s(\phi)=\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat\phi\|_2$
   of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] is not renormalized.
3. The product $\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal Fu$ is distributional
   multiplication of $\mathcal Fu$ by the smooth polynomially bounded bracket
   weight, not an a priori pointwise product; and $H^s$ elements are completion
   classes, not initially assumed to be functions.

$(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{s/2}$, and no pointwise value of $g$ at an individual
frequency is asserted before $g$ is obtained from the defining condition.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.

$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive sesquilinear form (bilinear over $\mathbb R$), and $F$ a bounded functional with the test-linearity required by $a$. Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with norm $\|\cdot\|_h$, not necessarily a subspace of $V$. Suppose the algebraic sum $X_h=V+V_h$ is equipped with a norm extending these norms, and $\widetilde a_h:X_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded sesquilinear extension of a discrete form $a_h$ with bound $M_h$. Over $\mathbb C$, both forms are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; over $\mathbb R$, they are bilinear. Assume $a_h$ is coercive on $V_h$ with constant $\alpha_h>0$, and let $F_h$ be bounded on $V_h$ with the matching test-linearity. The exact and discrete equations have unique solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+M_h/\alpha_h)\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\alpha_h,$$

where $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|/\|w_h\|_h$ when $V_h\ne\{0\}$, and $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u):=0$ when $V_h=\{0\}$. The estimate requires the bounded extension and does not assert that every nonconforming, penalty, or discontinuous Galerkin form has one.

For a family of these problems, suppose $M_h\le\overline M<\infty$ and $\alpha_h\ge\underline\alpha>0$ uniformly. Writing $E_h=\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h$, the uniform bound is
$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+\overline M/\underline\alpha)E_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\underline\alpha.$$
Thus uniform control of $E_h$ and $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ gives a uniform error budget; if both tend to zero, the errors tend to zero, and if both are $O(h^p)$ for a fixed $p>0$, the error is $O(h^p)$. No rate is inferred without those approximation, residual, and stability bounds.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For every $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, with $\Gamma$ as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], there is a unique $u=S\lambda\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying the weak single-layer equation of [[def-bem-laplace-layer-potentials-and-energy-spaces]]. It is harmonic on $\Omega^-$ and $\Omega^+$, its two traces agree, and its weak conormal traces satisfy
$$\partial_n^-u-\partial_n^+u=\lambda\quad\hbox{in }H^{-1/2}(\Gamma).$$
The trace operator $V\lambda:=\gamma u$ maps $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ boundedly into $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, and there are constants $C,c>0$ depending on $\Gamma$ such that
$$\|u\|_{\dot H^1}+\|V\lambda\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}},\qquad \langle\lambda,V\lambda\rangle_\Gamma\ge c\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2.$$
If $\lambda\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ (in particular for facewise smooth densities reaching edges or discontinuous P0 densities), this weak potential agrees away from $\Gamma$ with $\int_\Gamma(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}\lambda(y)dS_y$.

Let $\Gamma$ be a polyhedral boundary as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. A **conforming surface triangulation** $\mathcal T_h$ is a finite collection of nondegenerate closed planar triangles covering $\Gamma$, with disjoint relative interiors, such that two distinct triangles meet only in a common full edge, a common vertex, or not at all. For $T\in\mathcal T_h$, write $h_T=\operatorname{diam}(T)$ and let $\rho_T$ be the radius of the largest disk contained in $T$; the family is **shape regular** if $\sup_{h,T}h_T/\rho_T<\infty$, and **quasi-uniform** if $\inf_{h,T}h_T/h>0$ for $h=\max_{T\in\mathcal T_h}h_T$.

The conforming **P0 density space** is $X_h=\{\lambda_h\in L^2(\Gamma):\lambda_h|_T\text{ is constant for every }T\in\mathcal T_h\}$. The continuous inclusion $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Gamma)$ follows because each chart Bessel norm controls its L2 norm and the fixed partition is finite. Hence every $\lambda_h$ defines a bounded functional $v\mapsto\int_\Gamma\lambda_hv$ on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$; thus $X_h\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. This inclusion makes the single-layer Galerkin method conforming in its energy space.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal T_h$ and $X_h$ be the surface mesh and P0 space from [[def-bem-surface-mesh-and-piecewise-constant-density-space]]. For an ordered target/source pair $(T,S)$ define its exact 3D Laplace single-layer matrix entry by
$$A_{TS}=\langle1_T,V1_S\rangle_\Gamma=\int_T\int_S\frac{1}{4\pi|x-y|}\,dS_y\,dS_x,$$
where the equality is proved for every panel pair by [[lem-bem-panel-pair-duffy-certificates]]. Supply a positive per-entry tolerance $\tau_{TS}$ and construct exactly one auditable certificate as follows.

- **Near certificate.** For coincident panels or panels sharing an edge or vertex, use the finite sign-cell/pulling-simplex identity of [[lem-bem-panel-pair-duffy-certificates]]. A disjoint pair may also use that lemma's smooth fallback whenever the whole-panel far-cluster condition below is unavailable. Each term is a reference-triangle integral $\int_R|z|^{-\alpha_m}q_m(z)dz$ with $\alpha_m<2$ and transformed amplitude $G_m\in C^{2n}([0,1]^2)$. Record the exact change-of-variables derivation, the supplied derivative bounds, and the positive Gaussian remainder $E_m$ from [[cor-duffy-weighted-product-gauss-error]]. If $\rho_m$ is the separately certified total of nested fiber, node-value and outward arithmetic radii, require $\varepsilon_{TS}^{\rm near}=\sum_m|c_m|(E_m+\rho_m)\le\tau_{TS}$. A custom near identity is usable only after its identity and every Gaussian hypothesis have been fully verified. For the standard panel-pair construction, every final exponent is $\alpha_m=0$.

- **Far certificate.** For disjoint panels, choose positive centroid rules on finite midpoint subdivisions and use [[lem-bem-far-panel-quadrature-residual]] to record the physical-kernel quadrature residual $\varepsilon_{TS}^{\rm quad}$ and any separate outward evaluation radius $\varepsilon_{TS}^{\rm eval}$. If the source nodes with physical charges $q_j=v_j/(4\pi)$ lie in $B(c,a)$ and the target nodes lie in $B(d,b)$ with the strict condition $R=|d-c|>a+b$, evaluate the single-cluster field of [[alg-three-dimensional-laplace-cluster-expansion]]. For $Q=\sum_j|q_j|$ and target weight sum $W_T$, record
$$\varepsilon_{TS}^{\rm far}=\varepsilon_{TS}^{\rm quad}+\varepsilon_{TS}^{\rm eval}+W_T\frac{Q}{R-b}\frac{(a/(R-b))^{p+1}}{1-a/(R-b)}+\varepsilon_{TS}^{\rm FMM-arith}.$$
The final term is the outward arithmetic radius of the finite cluster evaluation; it is zero only for an exact-arithmetic evaluation. If the whole-panel balls fail $R>a+b$, do not use this tail and instead use the disjoint smooth near fallback. No global multilevel or $O(N)$ work claim is made.

For every pair require its certified total error $\varepsilon_{TS}\le\tau_{TS}$. Given one successful certificate for every ordered pair, form $\widetilde A_h=(\widetilde A_{TS})$. If $\gamma_h>0$ is a certified lower norm bound satisfying
$$\|c\|_2\le\gamma_h^{-1}\left\|\sum_Tc_T1_T\right\|_{H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)},$$
then the matrix defect is bounded by
$$\delta_h=\gamma_h^{-2}\left(\sum_{T,S}\varepsilon_{TS}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
Any missing or unverified panel-pair geometry, identity, derivative bound, arithmetic radius or certificate returns **uncertified** and no matrix-defect claim. In particular, the batch-26 Duffy rule alone does not certify arbitrary coincident or edge-adjacent pairs.

routine_steps.claim: Apply [F1] with exact form $a$, exact load $F$, and conforming subspace $X_h$. It gives the unique exact solution $u$, the unique exact Galerkin solution $u_h$, and $\|u-u_h\|_H\le(1+C/c)\inf_{v_h\in X_h}\|u-v_h\|_H$, since the consistency defect is zero.

The perturbation bound and coercivity of $a$ imply $\widetilde a_h(v_h,v_h)\ge(c-\delta)\|v_h\|_H^2$ for all $v_h$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Gamma$ be a polyhedral boundary as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. A **conforming surface triangulation** $\mathcal T_h$ is a finite collection of nondegenerate closed planar triangles covering $\Gamma$, with disjoint relative interiors, such that two distinct triangles meet only in a common full edge, a common vertex, or not at all. For $T\in\mathcal T_h$, write $h_T=\operatorname{diam}(T)$ and let $\rho_T$ be the radius of the largest disk contained in $T$; the family is **shape regular** if $\sup_{h,T}h_T/\rho_T<\infty$, and **quasi-uniform** if $\inf_{h,T}h_T/h>0$ for $h=\max_{T\in\mathcal T_h}h_T$.

The conforming **P0 density space** is $X_h=\{\lambda_h\in L^2(\Gamma):\lambda_h|_T\text{ is constant for every }T\in\mathcal T_h\}$. The continuous inclusion $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Gamma)$ follows because each chart Bessel norm controls its L2 norm and the fixed partition is finite. Hence every $\lambda_h$ defines a bounded functional $v\mapsto\int_\Gamma\lambda_hv$ on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$; thus $X_h\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. This inclusion makes the single-layer Galerkin method conforming in its energy space.

For $x\ne y$ in $\mathbb R^3$, the Newton kernel is $G_3(x,y)=(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}$. Its distributional fundamental-solution property $-\Delta_xG_3(x,y)=\delta_y$ is proved in [[lem-bem-newtonian-kernel-is-fundamental-solution]]. The kernel fixes the sign and $4\pi$ normalization for every three-dimensional layer operator on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For every $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, with $\Gamma$ as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], there is a unique $u=S\lambda\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying the weak single-layer equation of [[def-bem-laplace-layer-potentials-and-energy-spaces]]. It is harmonic on $\Omega^-$ and $\Omega^+$, its two traces agree, and its weak conormal traces satisfy
$$\partial_n^-u-\partial_n^+u=\lambda\quad\hbox{in }H^{-1/2}(\Gamma).$$
The trace operator $V\lambda:=\gamma u$ maps $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ boundedly into $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, and there are constants $C,c>0$ depending on $\Gamma$ such that
$$\|u\|_{\dot H^1}+\|V\lambda\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}},\qquad \langle\lambda,V\lambda\rangle_\Gamma\ge c\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2.$$
If $\lambda\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ (in particular for facewise smooth densities reaching edges or discontinuous P0 densities), this weak potential agrees away from $\Gamma$ with $\int_\Gamma(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}\lambda(y)dS_y$.

For $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ define the Laplace Calderon boundary operators by
$$V\lambda=\gamma S\lambda,\qquad K\phi=\tfrac12(\gamma^-D\phi+\gamma^+D\phi),$$
$$K'\lambda=\tfrac12(\partial_n^-S\lambda+\partial_n^+S\lambda),\qquad W\phi=-\partial_n^-D\phi=-\partial_n^+D\phi.$$
Here $\gamma S\lambda$ is the common trace, conormal traces use the orientation of [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], and the last equality is meaningful because the weak double layer has a common conormal derivative. This page uses the real duality pairing between $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$. The well-definedness and bounded mapping properties of $V,K,K',W$ are proved in [[thm-bem-calderon-mapping-and-jump-identities]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and that $\Gamma$ is polyhedral as specified in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. The interior trace $\gamma^-:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. On every bounded exterior boundary collar $C=\Omega^+\cap U$, where $U$ is a bounded neighborhood of $\Gamma$ with Lipschitz collar boundary, the exterior trace $\gamma^+:H^1(C)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. The corresponding localized assertion holds over each boundary chart. Thus an exterior function has this trace whenever it is $H^1$ up to the boundary on such collars; membership in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+)$ alone does not assert a boundary trace. There is a bounded linear right inverse $L:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\gamma(Lg)=g$. There is also a bounded extension operator $E:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $(Eu)|_{\Omega^-}=u$.

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ denote the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. Its elements have an $L^6$ representative, the trace $\gamma:\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded, and the right inverse above may be chosen with compact support near $\Gamma$.

Let $S=[0,1]^2$ and let $T=\{(x,y):0\le y\le x\le1\}$ be the reference triangle. The **vertex Duffy map** is $D:S\to T$, $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$. Its image, inverse for $r>0$, and Jacobian determinant are verified in [[lem-duffy-reference-map-jacobian-and-image]]. The change-of-variables use and endpoint limit for weak singularities are proved in [[thm-duffy-weak-singularity-transform]].

Let $\alpha<2$ and let $q:T\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. On $T\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ put $f(x,y)=\|(x,y)\|_2^{-\alpha}q(x,y)$, where $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm. The improper integral over $T$ is absolutely convergent and
$$\int_T f(x,y)\,dx\,dy=\int_0^1\int_0^1 r^{1-\alpha}G(r,s)\,ds\,dr,
\qquad G(r,s)=(1+s^2)^{-\alpha/2}q(r,rs).$$
In particular, the transformed radial weight $r^{1-\alpha}$ is integrable at zero because $1-\alpha>-1$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\alpha<2$, put $\rho=1-\alpha>-1$, and let $n\ge1$. For a continuous amplitude $G$ on $[0,1]^2$, let $(z_j,w_j)_{j=1}^n$ be the Gauss–Jacobi rule for weight $(1+t)^\rho$ on $[-1,1]$, and $(\zeta_i,v_i)_{i=1}^n$ the rule for weight $1$ there. Map nodes and weights to $[0,1]$ by
$$r_j=(1+z_j)/2,\quad a_j=2^{-(\rho+1)}w_j,\qquad s_i=(1+\zeta_i)/2,\quad b_i=v_i/2.$$
The **Duffy weighted product rule** is
$$Q_{n,\alpha}^{D}(G)=\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^n a_jb_iG(r_j,s_i).$$
It approximates $\int_0^1\int_0^1r^{1-\alpha}G(r,s)\,ds\,dr$, the transformed integral of [[thm-duffy-weak-singularity-transform]]. The finite nodes and weights are well-defined by the supplied Gauss–Jacobi rule; the error estimate is [[cor-duffy-weighted-product-gauss-error]].

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**

routine_steps.claim: Parametrize $T$ and $S$ by affine maps $t(u)$ and $s(v)$ from $\Delta_2=\{(u_1,u_2):u_i\ge0,\ u_1+u_2\le1\}$. Their constant surface Jacobians are $J_T=|(t_1-t_0)\times(t_2-t_0)|$ and $J_S=|(s_1-s_0)\times(s_2-s_0)|$. With $L(u,v)=t(u)-s(v)$ on $P=\Delta_2\times\Delta_2$, the nonnegative change of variables in [F8] gives $\mathcal I_{TS}=(J_TJ_S/(4\pi))\int_P|L(z)|^{-1}dz$, initially allowing an infinite value. The zero set $Z=P\cap L^{-1}(0)$ is the parameterized diagonal of $T\cap S$ and has dimension $2$, $1$, or $0$ for coincident, edge-sharing, or vertex-sharing panels.

Cut $P$ by each non-identically-zero coordinate hyperplane $L_i=0$. Enumerate each cell’s finitely many vertices by active boundary-hyperplane sets, discarding infeasible intersections. The at most eight resulting full-dimensional sign cells cover $P$ up to their boundaries; those boundaries are contained in finitely many hyperplanes and have four-dimensional measure zero by Fubini in [F8]. For any $z_0\in Z$ and interior point $z$ of a sign cell, $L((1-t)z_0+tz)=tL(z)$ for $0<t\le1$, so every $z_0$ belongs to that cell's closure. The simultaneous zero set of its signed nonnegative affine coordinates is therefore a nonempty face.

Triangulate each cell by pulling from a global vertex ordering that lists all vertices in $Z$ first and uses the same induced order on shared faces. The pulling induction is complete: for any point other than the first vertex, extend the segment from that vertex through the point to its last point in the cell; the exit point lies on a facet not containing the first vertex, so cones over those facets cover the cell, and overlaps occur only on their boundaries. Induction triangulates those facets and the common induced ordering makes adjacent cell triangulations agree. Every full-dimensional cell has a vertex in its nonempty face $Z$, hence its first vertex is in $Z$; each resulting four-simplex therefore has a zero vertex. In a simplex with signed affine coordinates nonnegative, their common zero set is exactly the convex hull of the zero vertices, so the zero face has dimension $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, covering all three contact types including coincident panels.

In a resulting four-simplex $\Sigma=[v_0,\ldots,v_4]$, order the vertices so exactly $v_0,\ldots,v_j$ lie in $Z$, put $d=3-j$ and $D=|\det(v_1-v_0,\ldots,v_4-v_0)|$, and define $B(b)=\sum_{m=j+1}^4b_mL(v_m)$ on the opposite face $\Delta_d$. That face contains no zero of $L$, so compactness gives $c=\min_{\Delta_d}|B|>0$. The join coordinates $z=(1-r)\sum_{i=0}^ja_iv_i+r\sum_{m=j+1}^4b_mv_m$, with $a\in\Delta_j$, $b\in\Delta_d$, and $0\le r\le1$, are one-to-one in the interiors and have absolute Jacobian $D r^{3-j}(1-r)^j$: the $j$ independent $a$ directions scale by $1-r$, the $d$ independent $b$ directions by $r$, and the radial column supplies $D$. Also $L(z)=rB(b)$.

The kernel times this Jacobian has radial factor $r^{2-j}(1-r)^j$. For $j=0,1,2$, $\int_0^1r^{2-j}(1-r)^jdr=(2-j)!j!/3!$ and $|\Delta_j|=1/j!$, so $\int_\Sigma|L(z)|^{-1}dz=D(2-j)!/6\int_{\Delta_d}|B(b)|^{-1}db$. This is finite because $|B|\ge c$. For $d=1$, split the unit square into its two triangles and swap coordinates on one to get $\int_0^1g(t)dt=\int_R(g(x)+g(y))dxdy$ with $g=|B|^{-1}$. For $d=2$, $(u,v)=(1-x,y)$ maps $R=\{0\le y\le x\le1\}$ onto $\Delta_2$ with determinant one. For $d=3$, set $u=1-x$, $v=y$, $w=(x-y)t$ on $R\times[0,1]$; the remaining barycentric coordinate is $(x-y)(1-t)$ and the Jacobian is $x-y$. Thus each case is a finite sum of reference-triangle integrals, including all zero-face dimensions, and each transformed amplitude is smooth near $R$ because its denominator is bounded below by $c$. The coefficients $c_m$ include the positive factor $J_TJ_S/(4\pi)$ from step 1.1 and the positive simplex determinants and radial factors above.

The positive bound $c$ is effectively certifiable from the finitely many vectors $L(v_m)$. Enumerate every nonempty face of their convex hull and solve the finite affine normal equations for the point nearest zero on its affine span, retaining feasible barycentric coordinates; a global minimizer lies in the relative interior of a smallest face and has zero tangential derivative there, so this enumeration finds the minimum. Row-reduce degenerate systems and include their lower-dimensional faces. Positivity follows from the zero-face characterization in step 4.1. For algebraic panel coordinates, exact algebraic comparisons and interval refinement yield a rational $0<\underline c<c$. For each polynomial parameterization $B(\xi)$ whose admissible domain lies in a unit cube and whose image lies in the image under $L$ of the opposite face, set $h=|B|^2\ge c^2$ on that admissible domain, $P_{0,0}=1$, out-of-range $P_{\beta,j}=0$, and $P_{\beta+e_i,j}=\partial_iP_{\beta,j}-(j-\tfrac12)P_{\beta,j-1}\partial_i h$. The product and chain rules inductively give $\partial^\beta h^{-1/2}=\sum_{j=0}^{|\beta|}P_{\beta,j}h^{-1/2-j}$; hence $M_\beta=\sum_j\operatorname{coefabs}(P_{\beta,j})\underline c^{-1-2j}$ bounds each required derivative there, since the absolute coefficient sum bounds a polynomial on the containing unit cube. Compose the triangle coordinates with the Duffy map before using a full square as the admissible domain; no positive denominator bound is asserted on an extension outside that image. Apply the finite Leibniz rule to polynomial prefactors such as $x-y$ and add the bounds for finite amplitude sums before using these estimates for $q_m$. Differentiation under the finite $t$ integral in the $d=3$ map is justified by these uniform bounds and the fundamental theorem of calculus.

For each smooth reference amplitude $q_m$ in step 5.1, the Duffy map $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$ from [F5] gives $\int_Rq_m=\int_0^1\int_0^1rG_m(r,s)\,ds\,dr$, $G_m(r,s)=q_m(r,rs)$. With $n\ge1$, the positive product rule in [F6] has error at most $K_1\|\partial_r^{2n}G_m\|_\infty+\tfrac12K_0\|\partial_s^{2n}G_m\|_\infty$, since $\int_0^1r\,dr=1/2$. The derivative bounds are computed in step 6.1; add the separately certified node-value, fiber, and outward-arithmetic radii with the coefficients $c_m$.

This bound gives effective termination. Fix $n=1$ and subdivide $R$ into similar triangles of maximum diameter $h$; after affine pullback the second pure derivatives of $q_m(A(r,rs))$ are bounded by $C h^2\|D^2q_m\|_\infty$, so the positive-rule errors sum to $O(h^2)$ after multiplying by the affine Jacobians, whose sum is one. Indeed, $D(r,s)=(r,rs)$ has $\partial_r^2D=\partial_s^2D=0$, so the pure second-derivative chain rules contain only the Hessian of $q_m$ and two factors from the affine map, each of size $O(h)$. Its nonzero mixed derivative is not part of the Gaussian remainder used here. In the $d=3$ fiber, composite midpoint quadrature on $M$ equal subintervals has error at most $B_{tt}/(24M^2)$ by the one-variable Gaussian remainder [F7]. Choose $h,M$ so these bounds consume less than half the requested tolerance, then refine outward interval enclosures for the remaining half. Exact algebraic input makes incidence, determinant, and strict-positive denominator decisions finite; every refinement terminates because the certified lower bounds are positive. With other coordinate formats, require supplied certified incidence, nondegeneracy, separation, and arithmetic bounds; absent or failed certificates return uncertified.

If $T,S$ are disjoint, $d_0=\operatorname{dist}(T,S)>0$. The parameter kernel $g(u,v)=|L(u,v)|^{-1}$ is smooth on $\Delta_2\times\Delta_2$ with denominator at least $d_0$. Compose $L$ with the Duffy parameterizations of both triangles; it is polynomial on a product of unit squares and still has norm at least $d_0$, so the recurrence of step 6.1 with a rational lower bound below $d_0$ supplies explicit uniform derivatives. Integrating over $v$ defines $q(u)=\int_{\Delta_2}g(u,v)dv$; differentiation under this finite integral is justified by those uniform bounds, and the simplex mass is $1/2$. The affine map $(u_1,u_2)=(1-x,y)$ sends the outer triangle to $R$. Evaluate each inner $v$ integral by the positive composite $\alpha=0$ Duffy rule; its error bound is uniform in $u$. Apply the outer rule of step 7.1 to $q$. Subdividing both reference triangles and using their computed second-derivative bounds makes the inner errors $O(h^2)$ uniformly in $u$ and the outer error $O(h^2)$; positivity and bounded total weight let these errors add. Thus the disjoint smooth fallback terminates at every positive tolerance, with its two numerical radii charged separately.

To identify the double integral with the weak matrix entry, use barycentric coordinates $(u_1,u_2,1-u_1-u_2)$ and cutoffs $\chi_n=\prod_{i=1}^3\min(1,nu_i)$ on each panel. They are bounded by one and converge almost everywhere and in $L^2$ to the panel indicator. By [F1], each cutoff is an $L^2$ density and the fixed $H^{1/2}$ chart norm controls $L^2$, so these cutoffs converge in $H^{-1/2}$ by duality; boundedness of $V$ in [F3] gives $\langle\chi_n1_T,V(\chi_n1_S)\rangle\to\langle1_T,V1_S\rangle$. For the trace identification, a finite union of planar faces satisfies $|\Gamma\cap B(x,r)|\le Cr^2$; dyadic annuli imply $\int_{\Gamma\cap B(x,\delta)}|x-y|^{-1}dS_y\le C\delta$. Splitting at distance $2\delta$ and using $|\nabla_xG_3|=(4\pi|x-y|^2)^{-1}$ gives continuity modulus $C\delta(1+|\log\delta|)$ for each bounded cutoff potential throughout a bounded neighborhood of $\Gamma$: the area and near-integral bounds are uniform for ambient target points, and the same near/far split applies there. By [F3] the off-surface kernel integral represents its weak potential; by [F4] its continuous restriction is its Sobolev trace, and Fubini [F8] identifies the pairing with the cutoff double integral. Absolute integrability from the touching-panel calculation in step 5.1 and the disjoint case in step 8.2 dominates these integrands, so dominated convergence gives $\langle1_T,V1_S\rangle=\mathcal I_{TS}$ for coincident, edge-sharing, vertex-sharing, and disjoint panels.

For $T\in\mathcal T_h$, write $h_T=\operatorname{diam}(T)$ and let $\rho_T$ be the radius of the largest disk contained in $T$; the family is **shape regular** if $\sup_{h,T}h_T/\rho_T<\infty$, and **quasi-uniform** if $\inf_{h,T}h_T/h>0$ for $h=\max_{T\in\mathcal T_h}h_T$.

The conforming **P0 density space** is $X_h=\{\lambda_h\in L^2(\Gamma):\lambda_h|_T\text{ is constant for every }T\in\mathcal T_h\}$. The continuous inclusion $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Gamma)$ follows because each chart Bessel norm controls its L2 norm and the fixed partition is finite. Hence every $\lambda_h$ defines a bounded functional $v\mapsto\int_\Gamma\lambda_hv$ on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$; thus $X_h\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. This inclusion makes the single-layer Galerkin method conforming in its energy space.

For $x\ne y$ in $\mathbb R^3$, the Newton kernel is $G_3(x,y)=(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}$. Its distributional fundamental-solution property $-\Delta_xG_3(x,y)=\delta_y$ is proved in [[lem-bem-newtonian-kernel-is-fundamental-solution]]. The kernel fixes the sign and $4\pi$ normalization for every three-dimensional layer operator on this page.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Fix $p\ge0$, source labels $J$ with positions $y_j\in\mathbb R^3$ and charges $q_j\in\mathbb C$, a center $c$, and a radius $a\ge0$ with $|y_j-c|\le a$. For each $0\le\ell\le p$, supply an orthonormal basis $\{Y_{\ell m}:-\ell\le m\le\ell\}$ of $\mathcal H_\ell$ from [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]]; its existence and dimension are given by [[lem-three-dimensional-laplace-spherical-harmonic-addition-theorem]]. Form moments
$$M_{\ell m}=\sum_{j\in J}q_j\overline{H_{\ell m}(y_j-c)}.$$
For every target $x$ with $r=|x-c|>a$, evaluate the truncated single-cluster multipole field
$$\widetilde U_p(x)=4\pi\sum_{\ell=0}^p\frac{1}{2\ell+1}\frac{1}{r^{\ell+1}}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}M_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}\!\left(\frac{x-c}{r}\right).$$
The output is an approximation to $U(x)=\sum_{j\in J}q_j/|x-y_j|$. This is the source-cluster-to-target evaluator only; it makes no 3D tree-translation or global all-target complexity claim.

For the arithmetic count, store each basis polynomial by its monomial coefficient array. Basis setup is done once for the chosen $p$. To evaluate the displayed formula directly, evaluate every basis polynomial by summing its monomials at each source and target point, then accumulate the moments and target sums. This convention makes the basis-evaluation work explicit rather than treating each special-function evaluation as free.

For the single-cluster evaluator of [[alg-three-dimensional-laplace-cluster-expansion]], let $Q=\sum_{j\in J}|q_j|$. If a target satisfies $r=|x-c|>a$, then its potential error obeys
$$|U(x)-\widetilde U_p(x)|\le\frac{Q}{r}\frac{(a/r)^{p+1}}{1-a/r}.$$
If a target region is contained in a ball of radius $b$ centered at $d$, with $R=|d-c|>a+b$, then every target in the region has error at most
$$\frac{Q}{R-b}\frac{\bigl(a/(R-b)\bigr)^{p+1}}{1-a/(R-b)}.$$
Let $S=|J|$ and let $T_0$ be the number of targets. Under the monomial-coefficient evaluation convention of the algorithm, forming moments and evaluating the truncated field costs $O((S+T_0)(p+1)^4)$ arithmetic operations after the basis coefficient arrays have been prepared. If all basis values at sources and targets are supplied, the coefficient accumulation and expansion evaluation alone cost $O((S+T_0)(p+1)^2)$. This is a single-cluster estimate; it is not a 3D multilevel FMM tree complexity theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and that $\Gamma$ is polyhedral as specified in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. The interior trace $\gamma^-:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. On every bounded exterior boundary collar $C=\Omega^+\cap U$, where $U$ is a bounded neighborhood of $\Gamma$ with Lipschitz collar boundary, the exterior trace $\gamma^+:H^1(C)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded. The corresponding localized assertion holds over each boundary chart. Thus an exterior function has this trace whenever it is $H^1$ up to the boundary on such collars; membership in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+)$ alone does not assert a boundary trace. There is a bounded linear right inverse $L:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\gamma(Lg)=g$. There is also a bounded extension operator $E:H^1(\Omega^-)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $(Eu)|_{\Omega^-}=u$.

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ denote the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. Its elements have an $L^6$ representative, the trace $\gamma:\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is bounded, and the right inverse above may be chosen with compact support near $\Gamma$.

Write $G_3$ for the Newton kernel of [[def-bem-newtonian-kernel-in-three-dimensions]]. For a smooth density $\lambda$ on $\Gamma$, the classical single-layer potential is
$$S\lambda(x)=\int_\Gamma G_3(x,y)\lambda(y)\,dS_y,\qquad x\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\Gamma.$$

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|
abla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$, using its $L^6$ representative and the trace from [[lem-bem-lipschitz-trace-and-lifting]]. For $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, consider the equation for $u\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}
abla u\cdot
abla v\,dx=\langle\lambda,\gamma vangle_\Gamma\qquad(v\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)).$$
Call such a function a weak single-layer potential and write $S\lambda=u$ when it exists. Define the exterior energy space $E^+(\Omega^+)=\{u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+):u\in L^6(\Omega^+),\ 
abla u\in L^2(\Omega^+)\}$. For a weakly harmonic function $u^-\in H^1(\Omega^-)$, define its weak outward conormal by $\langle\partial_n^-u^-,gangle=\int_{\Omega^-}
abla u^-\cdot
abla L^-g$, where $L^-g$ is any $H^1$ trace lift. For a harmonic $u^+\in E^+(\Omega^+)$, use the same fixed normal $n$ by $\langle\partial_n^+u^+,gangle=-\int_{\Omega^+}
abla u^+\cdot
abla L^+g$ for a compactly supported local lift. In either case the value is independent of the lift: the difference of two lifts has zero trace, and weak harmonicity makes its gradient pairing zero. The exterior formula also gives $\int_{\Omega^+}
abla u^+\cdot
abla v^+=-\langle\partial_n^+u^+,\gamma^+v^+angle$ for every $v^+\in E^+(\Omega^+)$. Indeed, subtract a compactly supported lift of $\gamma^+v^+$; the remaining zero-trace finite-energy function is approximated in gradient norm by compactly supported zero-trace functions using radial cutoffs: $\|v^+
abla\chi_R\|_2\le C\|v^+\|_{L^6(\{R<|x|<2R\})}	o0$. Boundary-chart flattening, zero extension, inward translation, and convolution approximate each zero-trace cutoff by interior smooth tests, so weak harmonicity makes its gradient pairing zero. This proves the energy identity without a flux assumption at infinity. Existence, uniqueness, agreement with the displayed kernel for smooth densities, and the conormal jump are proved in [[thm-bem-single-layer-transmission-mapping-and-coercivity]]. The weak definition fixes the normalization at infinity through $u\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$; arbitrary additive constants are excluded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is a constant $C(n,p)$ such that
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\mathbb R^n)}\le C(n,p)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$; here $|Du|$ is the Euclidean norm of the weak gradient.

For every $y\in\mathbb R^3$, the locally integrable kernel $G_3(x,y)=(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}$ of [[def-bem-newtonian-kernel-in-three-dimensions]] satisfies $-\Delta_xG_3(x,y)=\delta_y$ in the sense of distributions: for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}G_3(x,y)(-\Delta\varphi(x))\,dx=\varphi(y).$$

For $x\ne y$ in $\mathbb R^3$, the Newton kernel is $G_3(x,y)=(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}$. Its distributional fundamental-solution property $-\Delta_xG_3(x,y)=\delta_y$ is proved in [[lem-bem-newtonian-kernel-is-fundamental-solution]]. The kernel fixes the sign and $4\pi$ normalization for every three-dimensional layer operator on this page.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

For $t>0$ and $z\in\mathbb R^2$, let
$$P_t(z)=\frac{t}{2\pi(|z|^2+t^2)^{3/2}}.$$
Then $P_t\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ has integral one and, under the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier convention,
$$\widehat{P_t}(\xi)=e^{-2\pi|\xi|t}\qquad(\xi\in\mathbb R^2).$$

routine_steps.claim: By [F1], extension and a bounded-support cutoff put $u^-$ in $L^6(\Omega^-)$; $u^+\in L^6(\Omega^+)$ by definition. Thus $U\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$. Both pieces are $H^1$ in bounded boundary collars: on such a collar Holder gives local $L^2$ from $L^6$, and their gradients are already $L^2$. The fixed finite atlas also gives $\phi\in L^2(\Gamma)\subset L^1(\Gamma)$.

For a compactly supported smooth $\eta$, integration by parts for one weak derivative gives $\langle\partial_j U,\eta\rangle=\int_{\Omega^-}(\partial_j u^-)\eta+\int_{\Omega^+}(\partial_j u^+)\eta+\int_\Gamma\phi n_j\eta\,dS.$ Here is a polyhedral justification that introduces no hidden edge flux. In a graph chart integrate the vertical derivative by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem; for tangential derivatives use the graph change $x_3=t+\psi(x')$ and its piecewise affine chain rule. The graph boundary contribution is $(u^+-u^-)n_j\,dS$. A chart partition sums these formulas; derivatives of the partition cancel. $H^1$ approximation and bounded trace convergence from [F1] pass this formula from smooth chart functions to the given pieces. Internal planar-sector boundaries cancel because the restrictions of one $H^1$ function have the same interface trace. Only first derivatives are integrated and edges have surface measure zero; no derivative of the discontinuous face normal is taken. The imposed jump makes $u^+-u^-=\phi$. Taking the divergence of the displayed distributional identity, and using stationarity for the smooth global test $\eta$, gives $\langle-\Delta U,\eta\rangle=\int_\Gamma\phi\,\partial_n\eta\,dS.$

Put $P(x)=\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)\phi(y)dS_y$ off $\Gamma$. Since $|\partial_{n_y}G_3|\le(4\pi)^{-1}|x-y|^{-2}$ and $\int_{B_R(a)}|x-y|^{-2}dx\le CR$ uniformly in $a,y$, [F3] defines $P\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^3)$ and gives $\int_{B_R(a)}|P|\le CR\|\phi\|_{L^1(\Gamma)}.$ For the uniform ball estimate, if $|a-y|\le2R$ enclose the ball in $B_{3R}(y)$ and integrate radially; otherwise $|x-y|\ge|a-y|/2>R/2$, giving the same bound. Off $\Gamma$ all kernel derivatives are uniformly bounded on compact sets, so differentiation under the surface integral proves smoothness and harmonicity. Differentiating [F2] with respect to the source variable gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)(-\Delta\eta(x))dx=\partial_n\eta(y).$ This differentiation is valid distributionally: $|x-y|^{-2}$ is locally volume integrable, and integration by parts outside a ball of radius $\epsilon$ leaves a boundary term $O(\epsilon)$ for the first derivative of $G_3$. Fubini using that same local integrability therefore yields $\langle-\Delta P,\eta\rangle=\int_\Gamma\phi\partial_n\eta\,dS$.

Set $w=U-P$. Steps 2.1 and 2.2 show $\Delta w=0$ distributionally on the whole space. Choose a nonnegative unit-mass smooth bump $\rho$ supported in $B_1$ and let $w_\epsilon=w*\rho_\epsilon$. By [F4], $w_\epsilon$ is smooth and harmonic everywhere: $\Delta w_\epsilon(x)=\langle w,\Delta\rho_\epsilon(x-\cdot)\rangle=0$. Holder and step 2.2 give, for fixed $\epsilon$, $\int_{B_R(a)}|w_\epsilon|\le C(R+\epsilon)^{5/2}\|U\|_6+C(R+\epsilon)\|\phi\|_1.$ For a smooth harmonic $h$, differentiation of its spherical average gives $\frac{d}{dr}[(4\pi)^{-1}\int_{S^2}h(a+r\omega)d\omega]=(4\pi r^2)^{-1}\int_{B_r(a)}\Delta h=0$ by [F5]. Its limit at zero is $h(a)$, and radial integration gives the ball mean-value formula. Apply this to $h=w_\epsilon$ to obtain $|w_\epsilon(a)|\le |B_R|^{-1}\int_{B_R(a)}|w_\epsilon|\to0$ as $R\to\infty$. Thus $w_\epsilon=0$. Localizing $w$ to a slightly larger bounded set and applying the $L^1$ approximate-identity convergence of [F4] gives $w_\epsilon\to w$ in $L^1$ on every compact set. Hence $U=P$ almost everywhere. The smooth harmonic $P$ supplies the asserted representatives.

Fix a face-interior point $x$ and select a planar smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in that face and equal to one in a neighborhood of $x$. Split $\phi=\chi\phi+(1-\chi)\phi$. The second density is supported a positive distance from $x$, so its potential extends smoothly through a neighborhood of $x$ and has boundary value its kernel integral. For the first density, choose planar coordinates with outward normal $e_3$. Direct differentiation gives the potential $\frac12P_t*(\chi\phi)$ for $t>0$ and $-\frac12P_{|t|}*(\chi\phi)$ for $t<0$, where $P_t(z)=t/(2\pi(|z|^2+t^2)^{3/2})$. Its mass is one by [F5], while its mass outside each fixed disk tends to zero by direct radial integration. Uniform continuity of the compactly supported $C^1$ density therefore gives the two limits $\pm\phi(x)/2$, locally uniformly in the face interior. The same-face boundary kernel is identically zero, and the complementary integral is nonsingular near $x$, proving the claimed $K_{\rm ker}$ formula. Local uniform convergence also implies local $L^2$ convergence. On a compact tangential set $K$, parametrize either side by its nonnegative normal distance $t$. For $t>0$ the $H^1$ slice identity $\|f(\cdot,t)-\gamma f\|_{L^2(K)}^2\le t\int_0^t\|\partial_s f(\cdot,s)\|_{L^2(K)}^2ds$ follows from the fundamental theorem and approximation in [F1]; hence those same local $L^2$ limits are the Sobolev traces. Exhaust each open face by compact subsets; the finite edge and vertex set has area zero. This proves the almost-everywhere trace-average assertion.

Finally, facewise $C^1$ functions agreeing on shared edges are continuous piecewise $C^1$ in each piecewise affine graph chart. Their weak first derivatives are the bounded sectorwise derivatives: integration by parts on the planar sectors cancels all shared-edge boundary terms. After the chart cutoffs they belong to $H^1$ on $\mathbb R^2$, hence to its $H^{1/2}$ Bessel space by the Fourier weight inequality. Thus such densities satisfy the stated $H^{1/2}$ hypothesis even when nonzero at edges and vertices. No face-interior-core density assertion at the critical exponent is needed.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in
$\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and therefore depend only on the corresponding
almost-everywhere classes.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume Countable Choice. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, define
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\int_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|^2}{|x-y|^3}\,dx\,dy.$$
There is a finite constant $c_*>0$ such that
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=c_*\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\xi|\,|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi.$$
Consequently, the norm $\|f\|_2^2+[f]_{1/2,2}^2$ is equivalent on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ to the Bessel-potential norm $\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. The two completions therefore define the same $H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^2)$ space with equivalent norms.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Graph and chart distances and surface Jacobians are uniformly comparable, so the Slobodeckij double integral gives the corresponding $H^{1/2}$ norm comparison. A finite partition of unity and smaller chart cutoffs therefore transport the flat trace and lifts to the surface. Put $P_k=-\Delta-k^2$ and $G_k(x)=e^{ik|x|}/(4\pi|x|)$. Radial differentiation gives $P_kG_k=0$ for $x\ne0$. For $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, the distribution $T_\lambda$ defined by $T_\lambda(v)=\lambda(v|_\Gamma)$ (using the complex-bilinear distributional convention) is supported on $\Gamma$ and is in $H^{-1}(\mathbb R^3)$ by step 1.1. Consequently define $D_k\phi=S_kq-(1+k^2)G_k*f-f.$ For smooth $\phi$, the differentiated fundamental-solution identity and distributional convolution identify this expression away from $\Gamma$ with $\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)\phi(y)dS_y$. The first term is $H^1$ near $\Gamma$, the second is $H^2$ by step 2.1, and $f$ restricts to $F$ and zero on the two sides. This proves the asserted bounded piecewise $H^1$ extension and its uniqueness by density. It also shows its trace jump is $-\phi$.

Away from $\Gamma$, the kernel $G_k(x-y)$ and every target derivative are smooth in the ambient source variable $y$; after restriction to the $C^2$ surface they have uniformly bounded $H^{1/2}$ norms on compact target sets. The source normal in $D_k$ is $C^1$, which suffices for its integral against $\phi\in L^2$. Thus all target derivatives can be passed through these pairings and integrals, proving smoothness in $x$ there. Uniformly for bounded $y$ and $r\to\infty$, $G_k(r\omega-y)=O(r^{-1})$ and $(\partial_r-ik)G_k(r\omega-y)=O(r^{-2})$ together with any fixed finite number of $y$ derivatives; these follow by differentiating $|r\omega-y|=r-\omega\cdot y+O(r^{-1})$. The same estimates hold after one source normal derivative. The $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ norm of the first remainder is $O(r^{-2})$ by its uniform value and first source derivative bounds, so pairing with $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}$ proves the single-layer radiation condition. The double-layer radiation condition follows by integration against $\phi\in L^2(\Gamma)$ and the source normal derivative remainder bound. This proves all assertions.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in

almost-everywhere classes.

Assume Countable Choice. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, define
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\int_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|^2}{|x-y|^3}\,dx\,dy.$$
There is a finite constant $c_*>0$ such that
$$[f]_{1/2,2}^2=c_*\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\xi|\,|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi.$$
Consequently, the norm $\|f\|_2^2+[f]_{1/2,2}^2$ is equivalent on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ to the Bessel-potential norm $\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. The two completions therefore define the same $H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^2)$ space with equivalent norms.

routine_steps.claim: In surface coordinates put $r=|x-y|$. The $C^2$ graph bounds give $|n_y\cdot(x-y)|\le Cr^2$ and $|n_y-n_x|\le Cr$. Therefore both kernels $L_V=G_k(x-y)$ and $L_K=\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)$ satisfy $|L(x,y)|\le C/r$. Their first target-coordinate derivatives satisfy $|\partial_xL|\le C/r^2$: for $K$, differentiating the numerator tangentially gives $n_y\cdot t_x=(n_y-n_x)\cdot t_x=O(r)$, and differentiating the radial factors gives at worst $O(r^2)O(r^{-4})$. Fixed $k$ only changes the constants. Localize targets and sources by chart cutoffs; for near-diagonal pieces use a common graph chart and absorb its bounded surface Jacobian into the source kernel. Off-diagonal pieces have bounded first target derivatives. Each resulting chart kernel $l(z,w)$, extended with cutoffs by zero, thus has size $C/|z-w|$ and target derivative size $C/|z-w|^2$.

For a target translation $h$, $\delta=|h|<1/4$, consider $l(z+h,w)-l(z,w)$. Where $|z-w|\le2\delta$, integrate each size bound separately (including the ball around $z+h$), obtaining $C\delta$. On the complement the segment from $z$ to $z+h$ stays at distance at least $|z-w|/2$, so the derivative bound and polar integration give $C\delta\int_{2\delta}^{C}r^{-1}dr\le C\delta(1+|\log\delta|)$. This bounds both the supremum over $z$ of its absolute integral in $w$ and the supremum over $w$ of its absolute integral in $z$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the weighted kernel integral then proves the Schur estimate $\|Tf\|_2\le C\|f\|_2$ and $\|(Tf)(\cdot+h)-Tf\|_2\le C\delta(1+|\log\delta|)\|f\|_2.$ Indeed $|\int lf|^2\le(\int|l|)(\int|l||f|^2)$ and integration uses the two bounds. The cutoff support is fixed and bounded.

For any $0<s<1$, integrate the square of the last translation bound against $|h|^{-2-2s}dh$ for $|h|<1$; polar coordinates give the finite integral $C\int_0^1r^{1-2s}(1+|\log r|)^2dr$. The $|h|\ge1$ part is bounded by the $L^2$ estimate. Hence each localized $T$ maps $L^2$ boundedly to $H^s$ in the difference norm, in particular for $s=3/4$. To check the equivalent Fourier norm directly, apply Plancherel to differences and Tonelli: the inner integral $\int|e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot h}-1|^2|h|^{-2-2s}dh$ equals $c_s|\xi|^{2s}$ by scaling and rotation, with $0<c_s<\infty$ since near zero the numerator is $O(|h|^2)$ and at infinity it is bounded. This also identifies the half-order norm in [F3].

A bounded family of functions supported in a fixed compact chart and bounded in $H^{3/4}$ is precompact in $H^{1/2}$. Here is a direct verification. For a smooth compactly supported mollifier $\rho_\epsilon$, $|1-\widehat\rho(\epsilon\xi)|\le C\min(\epsilon|\xi|,1)$ and thus $\|f-\rho_\epsilon*f\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\epsilon^{1/4}\|f\|_{H^{3/4}}$ by the Fourier weights. For fixed $\epsilon$, the convolutions and their first two derivatives are uniformly bounded and have one fixed bounded support, by Cauchy–Schwarz with the fixed derivatives of $\rho_\epsilon$. They are precompact in $C^1$ on a containing rectangle: choose increasingly fine finite grids, take convergent subsequences of the finitely many value and first-derivative samples, and use the uniform first/second derivative bounds to extend sample convergence uniformly. A diagonal subsequence gives convergence of both values and first derivatives. Uniform $C^1$ convergence on a fixed compact support implies $H^{1/2}$ convergence, since the difference-norm integrand near the diagonal is bounded by $\|\nabla f\|_\infty^2|z-w|^{-1}$ and away from the diagonal by a constant times $\|f\|_\infty^2|z-w|^{-3}$. The uniform mollification error now gives finite nets for the original family in $H^{1/2}$, hence compact closure in its complete Hilbert norm.

Since $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ embeds boundedly in $L^2(\Gamma)$, steps 1.1–4.1 and the finite chart partition make both boundary integrals compact on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$. The single-layer integral agrees on smooth densities with $V_k$ of [F1]. For smooth densities, the normal-slice limits computed in [F2] are the Sobolev traces of [F1]: the planar half-Poisson terms have uniformly bounded mass, and the integrable $C/r$ curvature remainders and smooth-density remainders have uniform integral bounds on the compact surface, so the pointwise slice limits also converge in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. The normal-slice estimate proved in [F1] identifies this $L^2$ limit with the weak trace. Consequently [F2] identifies the double-layer exterior trace with $\tfrac12I+K_k$. Boundedness and density extend both identities to every $H^{1/2}$ density. Therefore $A_{k,\eta}=\tfrac12I+K_k-i\eta V_k$, and its displayed compact perturbation follows by addition and scalar multiplication of the compact maps just proved.

If $T\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\Delta T=0$, there is a unique smooth harmonic $h$ with $T=T_h$.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be connected and open, and let $u$ be real or complex harmonic on $\Omega$. If $u$ vanishes on a nonempty open subset of $\Omega$, then $u$ vanishes identically on $\Omega$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

routine_steps.claim: Set $w(x,t)=e^{kt}u(x)$ on the connected open set $\Omega^+\times\mathbb R\subset\mathbb R^4$. Distributional differentiation gives $\Delta_{x,t}w=e^{kt}(\Delta_xu+k^2u)=0$. By [F4] it has a smooth harmonic representative. This implies $u$ has a smooth Helmholtz representative: the distributional identity $\partial_tw=kw$ is also a classical identity for this representative, so $w(x,t)=e^{kt}w(x,0)$, and comparison as distributions gives $u(x)=w(x,0)$.

Choose $a$ so large that $\overline{\Omega^-}\subset B_a$, and fix $r>a$. The annular domain $B_r\setminus\overline{\Omega^-}$ has inner boundary $\Gamma$ and outer sphere. Its weak Green formula [F1], tested with $u$, gives $\int_{B_r\setminus\overline{\Omega^-}}(|\nabla u|^2-k^2|u|^2)dx=\int_{|x|=r}\partial_ru\bar u\,dS-\langle q^+,\gamma^+u\rangle.$ The last term is zero by the zero trace. The left side is real, hence $J(r)=r^2\operatorname{Im}\int_{\mathbb S^2}\partial_ru(r\omega)\overline{u(r\omega)}d\omega=0$. Only the original obstacle boundary has zero trace; no zero trace is assumed on the enclosing sphere.

At this fixed $r$, both $u(r,\cdot)$ and $\partial_ru(r,\cdot)$ are smooth, so their ordered harmonic projections converge in $L^2$ by [F2]. Cauchy–Schwarz passes the inner product to the limit of finite orthogonal sums. By [F2]–[F3], this gives $J(r)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{\ell=0}^N\|c_\ell\|_2^2/k.$ Every summand is nonnegative and step 2.1 gives zero, so all $c_\ell=0$. Completeness in [F2] now makes $u(r,\cdot)=0$ in $L^2$, hence pointwise by smoothness. This holds for every $r>a$, so $u=0$ on $|x|>a$. No degree sum was interchanged with the radiation limit at infinity.

The harmonic lift $w$ of step 1.1 vanishes on $(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline{B_a})\times\mathbb R$, a nonempty open subset of $\Omega^+\times\mathbb R$. The latter is connected because $\Omega^+$ is connected by hypothesis. [F4] gives $w=0$ everywhere there, hence $u=w(\cdot,0)=0$ on $\Omega^+$.
